central_claim.note: Both halves: conservatives in liberal regions less hesitant and more boosted, liberals less hesitant regardless.

evidence.note: Online survey of 683 US participants (E1 without convenience sample, Qualtrics or dates; E2 without screening numbers). Climate from zip-code 2020 presidential results (E3).

key_findings.note: Hesitancy half of F1; the vaccination/boosting half is not stated.
Steeper association in conservative climates; liberal half in [2].
Conservative half of F3 (60% vs under 35%). 'Significantly more likely' is loose (the interaction was significant); not flagged.

scope_and_limits.note: Proxy that may overlap other regional variables (population density); quote gives the consequence.

flags.text: Says orientation and climate 'interact to influence COVID-19 vaccination'. The paper (p.7) calls it 'the first assessment of the potential interaction ... and COVID vaccination' and says it cannot assume causal or directional associations (p.10).

theoretical_positioning.note: Presents the study as the first test of the interaction (T2). Does not name the two prior literatures, so no T1.

interlocutor_claim.note: Rönn et al. (ref. 19) checked: correct. Vaccination-rate half of I3 (booster rates, ref. 20, missing), no stance stated.
